aa-renales.summary: Large arteries leaving each side of the abdominal aorta to supply the kidneys. About 20–25% of the cardiac output goes to the kidneys.
facts: Abdominal aorta (L1–L2, just below the SMA)
The right renal artery is longer and passes behind the inferior vena cava; at the renal hilum it divides into anterior and posterior branches
Inferior suprarenal artery, ureteric artery; inside the kidney segmental → interlobar → arcuate → interlobular arteries
Kidneys, part of the suprarenal glands, upper ureter
clinical: Renal artery stenosis (atherosclerosis or fibromuscular dysplasia) is a secondary cause of drug-resistant hypertension.
Segmental arteries are end arteries, so their occlusion causes a wedge-shaped infarct.
tus: Accessory (polar) renal arteries are common (~25–30%); being end arteries, their ligation causes a segmental infarct.
Renal artery stenosis results from atherosclerosis (older men, ostial) or fibromuscular dysplasia (young women, mid–distal 'string of beads').

a-iliaca-communis.summary: Vessels formed by the division of the abdominal aorta at L4; they give rise to the arteries of the pelvis and legs.
facts: Bifurcation of the aorta (L4, level of the umbilicus)
Descends downwards and outwards along the medial border of psoas; in front of the sacroiliac joint it divides into the internal and external iliac arteries

Internal iliac artery (pelvic organs, buttock, perineum) and external iliac artery (becomes the femoral artery under the inguinal ligament; gives the inferior epigastric and deep circumflex iliac arteries)
Pelvic wall and organs, gluteal region, lower limb
clinical: Leriche syndrome: aorto-iliac occlusion causing buttock claudication, impotence and absent femoral pulses.
The ureter crosses the iliac bifurcation; kidney stones can lodge at this narrowing.
tus: The external iliac artery becomes the femoral artery once it passes under the inguinal ligament; its branches are the inferior epigastric and deep circumflex iliac arteries.

a-femoralis.summary: The main artery of the lower limb; it passes under the inguinal ligament in the groin to the front of the thigh.
facts: Continuation of the external iliac artery (below the inguinal ligament)

Superficial in the femoral triangle (femoral nerve lateral, femoral vein medial), then descends in the adductor (Hunter's) canal and passes through the adductor hiatus to the back of the knee as the popliteal artery

Superficial epigastric artery, superficial circumflex iliac artery, external pudendal arteries, profunda femoris artery (medial and lateral circumflex femoral arteries, perforating arteries), descending genicular artery
Thigh, hip (partly), femoral head (medial circumflex femoral artery), region of the knee
clinical: The femoral pulse is felt in the groin just below the point midway between the ASIS and the pubic symphysis.
It is a common access site for cardiac catheterisation and angiography.
In peripheral arterial disease the superficial femoral artery is the most often affected segment (claudication).
tus: In the femoral triangle the femoral artery lies within the femoral sheath; the most medial compartment of the sheath is the femoral canal (lymphatics and Cloquet's node).
For femoral catheterisation the puncture must be below the inguinal ligament; puncture above it risks retroperitoneal bleeding.

a-poplitea.summary: Continuation of the femoral artery in the popliteal fossa; it is the deepest structure of the fossa.
facts: Continuation of the femoral artery (adductor hiatus)
Descends in the popliteal fossa directly behind the femur and the capsule of the knee joint; at the lower border of popliteus it divides into the anterior and posterior tibial arteries
Superior genicular arteries (medial, lateral), middle genicular artery, inferior genicular arteries, sural arteries
Knee joint (genicular anastomosis), calf muscles
clinical: The popliteal pulse is felt by deep palpation with the knee flexed.
Popliteal artery aneurysm is the most common peripheral aneurysm.
The artery can be injured in knee dislocations and must always be assessed.
tus: In popliteal artery entrapment syndrome the artery is compressed by the medial head of gastrocnemius.
Popliteal aneurysm is the most common peripheral aneurysm and is often bilateral.

a-tibialis-anterior.summary: Artery supplying the anterior compartment of the leg; at the ankle it becomes the dorsalis pedis artery.
facts: Popliteal artery (lower border of popliteus)
Passes to the front of the leg through the gap at the upper border of the interosseous membrane and descends in front of the membrane with the deep fibular nerve
Anterior tibial recurrent artery, anterior malleolar arteries; continues as the dorsalis pedis artery
Muscles of the anterior compartment of the leg, front of the ankle
tus: The anterior tibial artery reaches the anterior compartment through the gap at the upper border of the interosseous membrane and runs with the deep fibular nerve.

a-tibialis-posterior.summary: Artery supplying the posterior compartment of the leg and the sole of the foot.
facts: Popliteal artery
Descends under soleus with the tibial nerve; behind the medial malleolus (tarsal tunnel) it divides into the medial and lateral plantar arteries
Fibular (peroneal) artery – lateral and posterior leg, calcaneal branches, medial plantar artery, lateral plantar artery (plantar arch)
Posterior and lateral compartments of the leg, heel, sole of the foot
clinical: The posterior tibial pulse is felt behind the medial malleolus, between the malleolus and the Achilles tendon.
tus: In the tarsal tunnel the posterior tibial artery divides into the medial and lateral plantar arteries.

a-dorsalis-pedis.summary: Continuation of the anterior tibial artery beyond the ankle, supplying the dorsum of the foot.
facts: Continuation of the anterior tibial artery (front of the ankle)
Runs forward on the dorsum of the foot lateral to the EHL tendon; in the 1st intermetatarsal space it joins the plantar arch through its deep plantar branch
Lateral and medial tarsal arteries, arcuate artery (dorsal metatarsal arteries), deep plantar artery
Dorsum of the foot and dorsal surface of the toes
clinical: The dorsalis pedis pulse is felt just lateral to the EHL tendon; it is important in assessing peripheral arterial disease (in some people it is congenitally absent).
tus: The dorsalis pedis pulse may be congenitally absent in some healthy people.

v-cava-superior.summary: Large vein carrying deoxygenated blood from the head, neck, arms and upper chest to the right atrium. It has no valves.
facts: By the union of the right and left brachiocephalic veins behind the right 1st costal cartilage
Right atrium (level of the 3rd costal cartilage)
Azygos vein (from behind), brachiocephalic veins (internal jugular vein + subclavian vein)
About 7 cm
clinical: Superior vena cava syndrome (mostly compression by lung cancer or lymphoma): oedema of the face and arms, dilated veins of the neck and chest.
The tip of a central venous catheter should ideally lie in the lower part of this vein.
tus: SVC syndrome (mostly lung cancer or lymphoma) presents with oedema of the face and neck and dilated veins on the chest.
The lower half of the SVC lies within the pericardium; it opens into the right atrium at the level of the 3rd costal cartilage.

v-cava-inferior.summary: The largest vein of the body, carrying deoxygenated blood from all parts of the body below the diaphragm to the right atrium.
facts: By the union of the common iliac veins at L5 (to the right of the aorta)
Rises to the right of the spine, runs in a groove on the back of the liver and passes through the caval opening of the diaphragm (T8)
Lumbar veins, right testicular/ovarian vein, renal veins, right suprarenal vein, hepatic veins, inferior phrenic veins
The left gonadal and left suprarenal veins drain first into the left renal vein
clinical: In deep vein thrombosis and recurrent pulmonary embolism an IVC filter can be placed.
In pregnancy, compression of the IVC by the uterus when lying on the back can cause hypotension (supine hypotension syndrome); turning onto the left side relieves it.
tus: IVC filters are placed below the renal veins.
The part of the IVC behind the liver receives the hepatic veins directly (retrohepatic IVC).

v-jugularis-interna.summary: Large vein in the carotid sheath that collects most of the blood from the brain, face and neck.
facts: At the jugular foramen as the continuation of the sigmoid sinus (superior bulb)
Descends in the carotid sheath lateral to the carotid artery; lies under the sternocleidomastoid
Behind the medial end of the clavicle it joins the subclavian vein to form the brachiocephalic vein (venous angle – on the left the thoracic duct drains here)
Inferior petrosal sinus, facial vein, lingual vein, superior and middle thyroid veins
clinical: The jugular venous pressure (JVP) reflects right heart pressure; it rises in heart failure.
Central venous catheters are often placed in the right internal jugular vein under ultrasound guidance.
tus: The internal jugular vein continues the sigmoid sinus and begins at the jugular foramen, where the superior bulb lies.
The right IJV is preferred for central lines: it reaches the SVC by a straighter route and the thoracic duct is on the left.
